newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Siam City Bank goes for bond.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Siam City Bank goes for bond.

text.p: Siam City Bank interrupted the slumber in Asian debt markets Tuesday with a US$115 million five-year Eurobond.
The 7.375 percent bond was launched and re-offered at 99.474 to yield 100 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries.
J.P. Morgan Securities was the lead.

The deal was launched off the issuer's global medium-term note programme. The first issue off the programme was launched in January, when SBC Warburg set a US$100 million floating rate note issue for the bank.
That five-year FRN had a put option in year three. It was launched at par to float at 45 basis points over the six-month London Interbank Offered Rate. Fees were 25 basis points flat.
Closer to home, activity was dull.
Pidemco Land, a member of the Singapore Technologies group, said it has launched a floating rate note issue worth S$199 million.
Pidemco said DBS Bank is the sole manager and agent for the deal, which will be for a maximum of five years.
Hong Kong banks have received invitations from China Development Finance Co to join the HK$2.0 billion floating rate certificate of deposit issue for Bank of China.
The five-year certificates pay a margin of 35 basis points over the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate and, with fees, an all-in return of 41.5 basis points for top tier participants.

Bank of China said last week that the all-in return would be about 40 basis points, which would be in line with the return offered on similar issues for Standard Chartered Bank and HongKong Bank, the territory's other two note-issuing banks.
Application will be made to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to accept the certificates as eligible for its Liquidity Adjustment Facility, or discount window.
Eligibility for LAF makes an issue more attractive to banks because holders of the qualifying debt can engage in repurchase agreements with the monetary authority, increasing liquidity.
But bankers said relationship issues, and not pricing or LAF-eligibility, is what makes the deal a winner.
"Twenty banks joined the deal before it even launched, so I guess that means we're behind," quipped one syndicate manager at a Japanese bank who said his bank would participate
